wp01_quarry_debug: The backfill stall was initially believed to be a resource contention issue because four workers showed full CPU with a flat queue depth.

The root cause of the backfill stall was a missing lease on the wire queue batch processing path: no worker held a lease before starting a batch, so two workers could claim the same batch, each mark its own copy complete, and the batch would be replayed, stalling progress.
We will implement a lease-before-claim pattern with a single-owner lease row keyed by batch id (30-second expiry, compare-and-swap on completion).
Non-owners will back off for 60 seconds and then re-check the lease, giving crash recovery if the owner never completed.
The completion path will be guarded by the owner check, and no other part of the wire queue changes.
We set a backfill cutoff at September 30 to avoid re-ingesting events that landed after the incident window.
We will land the additive lease-table migration before the Friday maintenance window to keep the schema stable during a vacuum job.
The lease approach gives single-owner semantics without a distributed lock service — durable simplicity.
The non-owner backoff prevents silent event loss (the “losing the batch silently is how we lose events” point).
The hydrate stage was already audited and clean, so the fix is scoped to the wire queue only.
The October 15 freeze bounds the change — no scope creep.
Maya Chen now owns the ingest queue service after the old platform group split.
If the stall recurs, Tomas is the escalation point because he knows the queue internals from a previous incident.
The estimated processing time (2400 batches × 1 second per batch / 4 workers ≈ 10 minutes) fits inside the maintenance window.
The wire queue processes batches of five thousand events each.
The DB maintenance window is Friday at 2am.
wp02_lumen_refactor: Lumen auth is moving from team-scoped tokens to per-graph API keys so each graph gets its own credential and its own audit trail
The per-graph key migration was sketched after a cross-team token incident and signed off by the team
The current team tokens never expire, which is exactly how a leaked token stayed valid for weeks
Every graph key starts with the tt_ prefix and nothing else in the system may mint that prefix
The platform standard is the tt_ prefix with a random 32-byte secret after it
Reusing the platform tt_ prefix for graph keys keeps the operator mental model to a single key family
Every graph key gets a token lifetime of twenty-four hours and requires rotation on the boundary
Short-lived keys mean a leak is a one-day problem, not a quarterly audit finding
Legacy team tokens remain valid until the rotation window closes, but minting of new legacy keys stops the day we flip
Forcing every team to rotate on day one would break the pilot
Bluepeak Logistics is the pilot customer for the per-graph rollout; their integration team is small and they were already asking for scoped credentials
Per-graph keys change the issuer shape: the key encodes the graph id, not the team id, so the registry must resolve a key to exactly one graph
The registry service must resolve a key to exactly one graph, a change from the team-scoped resolver
Priya owns the registry service, inherited via the data platform handoff, and must be looped into the interface review before the resolver is touched
A revoked key fails closed with a 401, no fallback to team scope; a revoked key must be dead on the next request
Key-usage events are retained for ninety days, matching the rest of the audit log; shorter would leave incident questions unanswerable
A single-commit flip is rejected as too risky because the change touches issuance, resolution, and enforcement
Two-phase deploy: phase one mints graph keys with enforcement off, phase two flips enforcement after the sandbox org runs on them for a week
The admin screen is the only known remaining team-token assumption in lumen; it renders the team token on the settings page and will be replaced with a per-graph key table
Short-lived keys, fail-closed revocation, and ninety-day usage retention together constitute the audit story; each supports the others
The grace period (stop minting, keep honoring, revoke at window close) tempers the cutover risk
Two-phase deploy tempers the blast radius of a change spanning issuance, resolution, and enforcement
The migration plan still needs to be written and the phase flag scaffolded

wp04_aurora_perf: The aurora dashboard load endpoint's p95 hit 4.2 seconds yesterday afternoon, an order of magnitude past the customer-facing SLO
The p95 spike correlates with the October 5 release that added the related-memory sidebar; before that release p95 was comfortably under a second
For every visible memory row the dashboard fires one embedding lookup to rank related items, so a page with forty rows issues forty separate calls
The N+1 embedding calls blew up the p95: forty round-trips at even twenty milliseconds each is nearly a second before any ranking happens
Batch the embedding lookup into a single call per page instead of one call per row; the embedding service supports a batch endpoint
Cache the embedding results in memory with a ten minute TTL and refresh them ahead of the next view
The dashboard serves about forty thousand load requests per day across all customers, and the sidebar fires on most of them
Ship the fix behind a flag so p95 can be compared before and after without a full rollout; the flag defaults off until the perf review signs off
Felix runs the dashboard perf review since he owns the frontend budget
Felix flagged the sidebar as a risk in the design review, a warning that was not acted on
Stale related items are a risk if the underlying memory changes between refreshes
Invalidate the cache entry for a team whenever a write lands in that team's graph; writes are rare compared to reads so invalidation traffic is tiny
Write-triggered invalidation keeps the ten-minute TTL as a backstop rather than the primary consistency mechanism
The fix should get the p95 back under 800 milliseconds, the number promised to the account teams
The dashboard had been getting slower for months with no single identifiable cause; measuring it finally localized the regression to the sidebar's N+1 pattern
wp05_retro_writeup: The Bluepeak outage ran from 9:12am to 12:53pm on Monday, about three hours and forty-one minutes of degraded search.
The first signal was the error budget burn alert at 9:15am, three minutes after the deploy that introduced the bad configuration landed at 9:12am.
The initial investigation blamed the search index, causing forty minutes of reindex work before Aisha pushed the team to check the config diff.
The config partition was the root cause: the deploy shipped a config that split query traffic unevenly across the search shards and one shard saturated.
The mitigation was rolling the config back to the previous partition at 12:40pm; traffic normalized within thirteen minutes and search was fully healthy by 12:53pm.
The search SLO is 99.9 percent and we landed at 99.86 for the month, breaching it.
We offered Bluepeak a service credit and their account team accepted.
Add a pre-deploy check that compares partition weights against the shard capacity model.
Make the config diff visible in the deploy review.
Maya owns the pre-deploy check and it needs to land by November 2.
Diego owns the config diff surfacing, due November 9.
The search team will run a shard capacity review before the end of the year, Priya volunteered to lead it.
The rollback went smoothly because the deploy tooling kept the previous config one click away.
The on-call stayed calm under pressure.
Customer-facing status was posted at 9:40am and the all-clear at 1:05pm; Sam from customer engineering wrote the status updates with Aisha.
The retro will be published company-wide.
Incident writeups are opt-out by default, the decision after the August incident.
wp06_quarry_rollout: The lease-before-claim fix was believed scope-independent: the lease CAS makes duplicate processing impossible regardless of rollout shape
The chaos harness confirmed the lease guarantee holds at the shard boundary: killing lease-holding workers mid-batch on four shards produced zero duplicate claims after expiry
All-at-once rollout is safe and a week of per-shard canary watching buys nothing
The lease CAS is the mechanism: only the owner can complete a claim, so a second attempt fails at compare-and-swap regardless of what toggles around it
The original stall was a no-lease bug, not a flip bug, so the glitch scenario (a flip mid-rollout re-entering the race) is not a real risk once the lease is held
Ship the lease fix all-at-once behind a single global kill flag
One flag is one switch to pull, and the fix itself cannot re-race
Maya drives the flip — she owns the ingest queue service and ran the staging matrix
The lease migration already landed ahead of Friday's maintenance window
If we flip mid-rollout and the flip glitches, we could re-enter the duplicate-processing race while the queue drains
After the flip, watch the queue drain and pull the global kill flag on any regression
Flip rollouts should be driven by one person with the runbook open, not a group-chat decision at 2am
The chaos run took longer than expected because it was queued behind the nightly embedding job
wp07_bluepeak_followup: The global flag flip raced the lease renewal at region cutover, leaving a window where two workers could claim one batch.
The global flag toggle was two hours before the first duplicate.
The renewal stamps show no overlap and no double renewal.
The flag did not cause the duplicates.
Clock skew between regions makes lease expiry unsafe because the CAS compares against wall-clock expiry, so a drifted clock changes who wins.
The region clock drifted eleven seconds.
The eleven-second drift produced the six-minute duplicate window: the lease expired early, the second worker claimed the batch, and the hydrate side saw the duplicate.
The lease behaved as designed under a drifted clock.
A thirty-second grace period on lease expiry, sized to the worst observed drift, bounds the skew hazard without making the lease lax.
The SLO review's sub-second skew assumption is invalidated.
The SLO review assumed sub-second skew between regions.
The global flag is a single point of failure; one bad region becomes a fleet-wide event.
Reverse the all-at-once call; use per-service flags instead of one global flag.
Per-service flags architecture supersedes the global flag architecture.
The duplicates are attributed to clock drift, not to the rollout fix.
Priya will track the grace-expiry log for a week.
The hydrate queue will be re-run before the next rollout.
